node.label: Brenda Macdougall
node.date_label: One of the Family 2010 · Clio Prize 2011 · 'Ways of Knowing' symposium 2018 · open letter 2021
node.description: Historian of Métis family and community in the northwest. One of the Family (2010) set out 'to contribute … to the development of methodologies and models by which we could interpret historical documents in a manner that reflected the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'. She read fur-trade, mission and scrip records through wahkootowin, a concept she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell and frames as a Cree worldview of 'relatedness' that 'did not appear in any of the historical records'. Against a historiography 'overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture', she showed Métis people 'actively involved in becoming, rather than passively awaiting identity transmission through external forces and trauma'. In 2018 she co-hosted a symposium on Métis-specific research methods.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Brenda Macdougall; One of the Family: Metis Culture in Nineteenth-Century Northwestern Saskatchewan (UBC Press, 2010); 'Ways of Knowing: Promising New Directions for Métis Research' (Shekon Neechie, 2018). University of Saskatchewan (BA 1994, PhD 2005); University of Ottawa, Chair in Métis Studies from 2010.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reads fur-trade, mission and scrip records through wahkootowin, a concept absent from the records that she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell, so that documents can reflect 'the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: One of the Family, pp. xi–xii ('My intent … was to contribute in some fashion to the development of methodologies and models by which we could interpret historical documents in a manner that reflected the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'; the term 'did not appear in any of the historical records', and she credits it to Métis Elder Maria Campbell), p. 3 (her definition, briefly: relatedness with all beings), p. 11 (genealogical reconstruction as method; no genealogies reproduced). Her 2018 Shekon Neechie report (cited, not quoted) treats acknowledging the sources of ideas and stories as a research protocol.

proposed_edges.relationship: Canadian Métis historiography was 'overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture', classifying the Métis as 'more white or Indian, more French or British'; Giraud's analysis 'verged on the eugenic'.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: One of the Family, p. 14: 'Canadian scholarship tends to focus on how best to classify the Metis – were they more white or Indian, more French or British? In short, Canadian scholars, like their American colleagues, have been overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture'; p. 13 on Giraud; p. 2 on 'Red River myopia'. Fairness: Van Kirk and Brown's work is 'pioneering' (p. 13) and Spry is credited (p. 14). Ends in Agent A's field (parallel to A's Andersen critique of fur_trade_families_metis); A to confirm.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Maria Campbell has no people record or entry; the credit is recorded in the edge and description text only (OCAP review #6).
